title: Benchmark expands rare earth price assessments with 19 new grades
gist: Benchmark added 19 rare earth price grades (12 CIF North America, 7 DDP China) to show the gap between delivered Western and Chinese domestic prices, citing China at about 87% of refined rare earth supply in 2026 and widening export licensing.

insights.claim: China accounts for around 87% of refined rare earth supply and roughly two thirds of mined supply in 2026.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: Processing, not mining, is the chokepoint; ex-China refining is where the scarcity value sits.
insights.quote: China accounts for around 87% of refined rare earth supply and roughly two thirds of mined supply in 2026
insights.locator: According to Benchmark's Rare Earths Service

insights.claim: Beijing has introduced and widened export licensing on a range of rare earths, leaving buyers outside China with restricted availability, volatile pricing and few reliable reference points.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: Licensing drives a bifurcated market; expect continued price premia outside China.
insights.locator: Beijing has introduced and widened export licensing

insights.claim: Benchmark assesses delivered North American prices alongside Chinese domestic prices to show how wide the gap between the two has become and how it moves over time.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: The ex-China premium is a tradable signal of policy risk and the value of non-Chinese supply; track it for MP Materials-type producers.
insights.quote: By assessing delivered North American prices alongside the Chinese domestic market, we can show how wide the gap between the two has become and how it moves over time.

insights.claim: Twelve of the 19 new grades are CIF North America, reflecting a region relying increasingly on material from outside China, and seven are DDP China, showing the premium buyers pay outside China.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: New benchmarks make premium-based contracts and hedges possible.
insights.locator: What are the new rare earth price grades

insights.claim: The rare earth market has long been thinly traded and hard to read, especially for Western buyers.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: Thin liquidity means price spikes can be sharp; opacity favors those with market access.
insights.quote: The rare earth market has long been thinly traded and hard to read, especially for buyers in the West

insights.claim: CIF North America grades cover samarium, cerium, europium, lanthanum (two grades), ytterbium, gadolinium, lutetium, erbium, holmium and thulium oxides plus praseodymium-neodymium metal at 99.0%.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: Coverage extends beyond NdPr to heavier and minor rare earths where supply is tightest.

insights.claim: Praseodymium-neodymium metal is the key feedstock for permanent magnets used in electric vehicles, wind turbines and defence systems.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: NdPr pricing is the core exposure for magnet demand across EVs, wind and defence.
insights.locator: Praseodymium-neodymium metal is the key feedstock

insights.claim: Minor rare earths serve niche uses: cerium and lanthanum in catalysts, glass and polishing; europium in display phosphors; ytterbium, erbium, holmium and thulium in lasers and fibre optic amplifiers; gadolinium in medical imaging; lutetium in PET scan scintillators.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: Small niche markets are easily squeezed by export controls; price visibility helps identify bottlenecks.
insights.locator: Cerium and lanthanum are used in catalysts
